alignment.note: Greek λέγει is present tense ('says', historic present); Latin ait and Syriac ܘܐܡܪ (prefixed with the conjunction ܘ-) both render it as a simple past/aorist 'said', a routine smoothing of the Markan historic present into narrative past tense.

The Greek recitativum ὅτι introduces direct discourse and is normally left untranslated as such; the Vulgate represents it with a colon (:), while the Peshitta marks the quotation lexically with the relativising prefix ܕ- on the following verb ܕܟܠܟܘܢ. The Greek conjunction and the Latin colon are functionally equivalent quotation markers.
ἐν ἐμοί / ܒܝ / in me; the Syriac fuses preposition and pronoun into a single enclitic form.
ἐν τῇ νυκτὶ ταύτῃ / ܒܗܢܐ ܠܠܝܐ / in nocte ista; word order of the demonstrative differs (Greek/Latin postpose 'this', Syriac preposes ܒܗܢܐ), a minor stylistic feature.
Causal ὅτι / ܓܝܪ / quia; the Syriac postpositive particle ܓܝܪ stands after the verb, whereas Greek and Latin place the causal conjunction first.

γέγραπται (perfect) / ܟܬܝܒ / scriptum est; all three render the citation formula 'it is written', the Vulgate using the periphrastic perfect passive scriptum est plus a colon to open the scriptural quotation (cf. Zech 13:7).

The citation of Zech 13:7 appears in the first person singular future ('I will strike') in all three: πατάξω, Percutiam, and Syriac ܕܐܡܚܐ. The Peshitta prefixes the relativiser ܕ-, subordinating the quotation, where Greek and Latin leave it as independent direct speech.
τὸν ποιμένα / ܠܪܥܝܐ / pastorem; the Syriac marks the definite object with the prefixed ܠ-, paralleling the Greek accusative article.
καί / et; the connective is fused into the Syriac verb prefix (see next group).

Greek τὰ πρόβατα and Latin oves explicitly name 'the sheep' as the subject; the Peshitta lexicalises this as ܐܡܪܘܗܙ ('its lambs/sheep'), placing the noun after the verb and supplying a possessive suffix referring back to the shepherd, a syntactic recasting of the flock as belonging to the stricken shepherd.

διασκορπισθήσονται / ܘܢܬܒܕܪܘܢ / dispergentur; the Syriac verb carries the conjunctive ܘ- prefix (corresponding to Greek/Latin καί/et) and precedes its subject, whereas Greek and Latin place the verb after the subject 'sheep'.
